title: Harmony and Progressions
intro: Harmony on the guitar is the same Roman-numeral harmony as on the piano (see Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony)), but guitarists think of it through movable shapes, the capo and the Nashville number system.

blocks.text: Because barre shapes move, a key's chords sit in a fixed pattern on the neck. In G major with E-shape barre chords (root on string 6): I G at fret 3, ii Am at 5, iii Bm at 7, IV C at 8, V D at 10, vi Em at 12 (or open), vii° F♯° (rarely used). With A-shape chords the same key starts at C (IV) on string 5 fret 3. Mixing the two shapes keeps the hand near one area: G (E shape, fret 3), C (A shape, fret 3), D (A shape, fret 5), Em (E shape, open or 12).

blocks.text: Session players in Nashville write chord charts with numbers instead of letters: 1 4 5 1 for I–IV–V–I, with a minus or 'm' for minor (6m or 6–), a slash for inversions (1/3 = I with the third in the bass) and small diamonds or ties for rhythm. The chart works in any key, so the band can follow a singer who changes key at the session. It is Roman-numeral analysis written for working musicians.

Guitarists often choose a key by its shapes: the open-chord keys are C, G, D, A and E (and Am, Em, Dm). With a capo every key becomes an open-chord key. To play in E♭, use C shapes with the capo at 3, or D shapes at 1. Two guitarists often play the same song with different shapes and capo positions so their voicings complement each other.

items: I–IV–V (G–C–D), the basis of folk, country and early rock.
I–V–vi–IV (G–D–Em–C) and vi–IV–I–V, the pop loop.
I–♭VII–IV (D–C–G in D), the Mixolydian rock progression borrowed from the parallel minor (see Chromatic Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/chromatic-harmony)).
i–♭VII–♭VI–V (Am–G–F–E), the 'Andalusian cadence' of flamenco and much rock; the E at the end is a major dominant with G♯ from harmonic minor.
12-bar blues in E or A with dominant sevenths and a shuffle rhythm: alternating 5th and 6th above the root on the low strings (A5–A6 and so on), the Chuck Berry and Jimmy Reed pattern.

blocks.title: Nashville
blocks.text: Write the chord chart 1 – 5 – 6m – 4 in A major and in E♭ major.
solution: A major: 1 = A, 5 = E, 6m = F♯m, 4 = D.
E♭ major: 1 = E♭, 5 = B♭, 6m = Cm, 4 = A♭.

blocks.title: Capo
blocks.text: A singer wants a song in B♭. Which capo position lets you play it with G-shapes, and with A-shapes?
solution: From G to B♭ is 3 semitones: capo at 3 with G shapes. From A to B♭ is 1 semitone: capo at 1 with A shapes.
